Project #1: The Rolling Die
Due Sunday by 11:59p.m. Points 54 Submitting a file upload File Types zip, mp4, and txt Available until Oct 28 at 11:59p.m.
Project #1: The Rolling Die
This project is worth 18% of your final grade. This project covers material from weeks 1 through 5. The project involves implementing an application for a sample client, and a video component training them how to use it, justifying your design, and documenting your process.

Unlike the in-class activities, you are permitted to use AI tools to help create the source code for the implementation of the project. You are not allowed to use AI tools to help produce the video or its content. You are not required to use AI tools to complete the work, you can complete it manually if you prefer. A video portion of the assignment involves documentation and discussion of your process, and if you have used AI you will discuss this at this point. If you did use AI, that's completely OK, it's not something you need to hide with this project, as it's now a standard tool widely used in industry and this project may be an opportunity to get more experience using AI.

But please just be honest about using AI if you did, because it would still be considered an academic integrity breach if a student claimed they did not use AI when they did in fact use AI (similar to how not citing a source is an academic integrity breach, even if using sources is allowed). If you do use AI tools, you are required to maintain a log of the prompts and/or other inputs provided to the AI tool(s), so ensure that you do this from the outset of building your application.

 

About the Client
The Rolling Die is a small board game store and café with a loyal community that gathers both in-store and on their public Discord server to talk about games, ask about stock, and organize game nights. The owner, Priya, and her small staff currently answer all customer questions about inventory manually, and are looking for some help modernizing their operations.

 

Message from the Client
Subject: Website + Discord bot for The Rolling Die

Hi team,

Thanks for taking this on! Here's what we're hoping for.

We're a board game store and café downtown, and we've got a really active Discord server full of regulars who love asking about what we've got in stock, prices, that kind of thing. Right now my staff and I are answering all of that manually, which eats up a lot of time, especially during a busy Saturday.

What we need:

A simple website where my staff can log in and manage our game inventory, add new games, update details, change stock counts, remove things we don't carry anymore. Customers should also be able to browse what we have without needing an account, just to check what's available or look something up before they come in.

A Discord bot for our server that lets people ask about games directly in Discord, things like checking if something's in stock, or looking up the price, without having to message us. It'd be great if it could handle a few different kinds of questions people usually ask us, we get asked things like "do you have Wingspan" or "how much is Catan" pretty regularly, but feel free to think about what else might be useful for a shop like ours.

One more thing that would be really helpful, I'm often at the counter or in the back with staff, and I'd love if there was some kind of live view I could glance at showing when someone's using the bot, without needing to refresh anything. Not necessary to see everything, just enough to get a sense of when the bot's being used and for what. My nephew mentioned something about this being possible without a page refresh and I thought that sounded neat, so if that's doable I'd love to have it.

We trust you to figure out the best way to build all this, we're not techy people, so we'll leave the details up to you.

Thanks so much,
Priya
Owner, The Rolling Die

 

Technical Requirements
These are the minimum requirements your project must satisfy. How you meet them, beyond what's specified, is up to you.

Build the web application following the multipage MVC pattern used in class (Express, Mustache, with separate controller and model files).
Store all game data in a SQLite database. No data should be held only in memory.
Provide at least one public page where anyone can view the current game inventory without logging in. This page must not allow editing.
Provide a manager area that requires login to access. Only logged in users should be able to create, edit, or delete game entries.
Build a Discord bot with at least 3 slash commands that query your live game data, each accepting at least one required argument that affects the result (e.g. a game title to look up). If you want an extra challenge, you could add a command that takes multiple arguments (e.g. comparing two games, or filtering by category and price), but this isn't required.
Whenever the manager adds, edits, or deletes a game through the web app, the Discord bot's replies must reflect that new data immediately. Don't cache old data anywhere that would cause the bot to reply with stale information.
When the Discord bot receives and responds to a command, push a real time update over websockets to the manager's web dashboard reflecting that activity, without the manager needing to refresh the page. What information you show and how you display it is up to you.
Use git to track your progress throughout development, with regular, reasonably descriptive commits (not one single commit at the end). Include your full .git folder in your submitted zip, don't delete it the way you would delete node_modules.
 

Hint: Running the Bot and Web Server Together
Your Discord bot and your Express/websocket server can run in the same app.js file, as the same running program. Your bot's command handler can directly call the same io object your web server created to push an update, with no extra setup needed to connect the two. Roughly:

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
const http = require('http').Server(app);
const io = require('socket.io')(http);

const { Client, GatewayIntentBits } = require('discord.js');
const client = new Client({ intents: [GatewayIntentBits.Guilds] });

client.on('interactionCreate', async function(interaction) {
  if (!interaction.isChatInputCommand()) return;

  // handle your slash command, query your database, reply to the user

  io.emit('botactivity', { command: interaction.commandName, time: new Date() });
});

client.login('YOUR_BOT_TOKEN');

http.listen(3000, function() { console.log('Server listening...'); });

This is an illustrative sketch, not complete code, you'll still need to register your slash commands and handle them properly as covered in class.

 

Submission
You will submit the following:

1. Your source code, as a single .zip file named implementation.zip, including your .git folder. Delete your node_modules folder before zipping (but keep .git). Include a brief README with any setup steps needed to run your application (e.g. how to configure your bot token, how to initialize the database).

2. If you used AI tools while building this project, include a plain text file named ai_log.txt in your zip. For each significant prompt or other input provided to AI (e.g. markdown files, etc.), note which AI tool you used, roughly what you asked for or what the input was, and what you changed, fixed, or verified afterward as a result of reviewing what it gave you. The log file should effectively document all the major prompts and inputs provided to the AI, even if this means the file is large. Note that it's possible to setup tools like Claude Code to automatically store every prompt: https://gist.github.com/michaelewens/9a1bc5a97f3f9bbb79453e5b682df462Links to an external site.. If you did not use AI tools, you don't need to include this file, your git history takes its place instead.

3. One video, named either video.mp4 (if uploading the video file directly), or a plaintext file video.txt containing a single unlisted YouTube link (if hosting it there instead). Your video must be no longer than 10 minutes. Clearly announce the start of each of the following three sections in the video itself (e.g. state out loud "starting the training walkthrough now") so your instructor can navigate it easily:

Training walkthrough (approximately 4 minutes): Demonstrate your application as if training a new staff member at The Rolling Die. Show the manager area being used to add, edit, or remove a game, and show the Discord bot reflecting that change when queried. Show the live dashboard update when the bot is used. This should naturally demonstrate that your minimum technical requirements are met, you don't need to narrate the requirements checklist directly.
Design justification (approximately 3 minutes): Explain the choices you made in meeting the client's needs.  For example, you might discuss why you structured the manager area or public page the way you did, what informed your choice of Discord bot commands, or what you decided to show on the live dashboard and why, but you don't need to address every part of the app equally, focus on whichever decisions best show your reasoning.
Process documentation (approximately 3 minutes): If you used AI tools, walk through several entries from your ai_log.txt and discuss which tool you used, what you asked for, and how you refined or verified what it gave you (e.g. you found a bug and re-prompted, you were unsatisfied with the output for some reason, or you tested the code and had to fix something yourself). If you did not use AI tools, reference specific commits from your git history (by commit message or hash) and discuss in detail where you got stuck, what bugs you ran into, and how you resolved them over time.
